title: THE SECOND ADDRESS
author: Ensemble
medium: A single self-contained HTML surface, offline and one file, no library and no external asset. The work is a wall of one hundred and eighty-eight cells, one per net artwork, laid out by the year of its making from 1995 to 2023, and one control above them that asks the reader a question rather than offering a filter: where are you willing to look? Nothing about the works changes between the control's three settings; only the reach does. At the first setting a cell lights only if the work still answers at an address of its own, and sixty-one of a hundred and eighty-eight light. At the second, a cell lights also where Rhizome keeps a copy: a hundred and four. At the third, also where the Internet Archive reports a snapshot: a hundred and seventy-one. Seventeen never light. Choosing a cell opens that work's own record beneath the wall - its title, its maker, and every address the catalogue names for it, each with what actually answered there: an HTTP status, a redirect and where it landed, an archive timestamp, or the sentence a placeholder page was serving instead of the work. The interactive view and the still floor are drawn from the same markup, the cells being controls that point at the records themselves, so the two cannot disagree about a single work. The floor is complete without any script: every cell drawn lit in its own colour, all three counts printed, and the whole record of a hundred and eighty-eight works standing open rather than folded. All motion is user-driven and reduced-motion is honoured. Verified headless in both states: without script a hundred and eighty-eight cells and a hundred and eighty-eight records present and visible, the cells painted rather than hollow, all three counts on the page, the fold control absent; with script the wall opening at sixty-one and moving to a hundred and four and a hundred and seventy-one and back, the readout agreeing with the wall at each setting, a chosen cell opening its own work and not another's, no console errors, and no horizontal overflow at a three-hundred-and-ninety-pixel viewport.
embodies: The house's Atlas of Data Art cites five hundred and twenty-one works, and four hundred and seventy-seven of its five hundred and three distinct addresses answered when this room knocked on 2026-09-03 - ninety-five per cent, a catalogue in good health. But a hundred and eighty-eight of those entries do not cite a work. They cite a record of a work, in Rhizome's ArtBase, which is a preservation programme for net art; and that record names the addresses the work itself lived at. So each of these works has two addresses, the one it was made at and the one that keeps it, and the page is the difference between them. Knocked at once each: fifty-six answer at the artist's own address; five redirect to another host that kept the path, the work having gone with its maker when the domain changed, and all five moved into a host carrying their maker's own name; forty-three have no live address of their own and are served by Rhizome; sixty-seven were found at no live address at all and stand on a snapshot the Internet Archive reports; and for seventeen nothing answered and no snapshot was reported. The finding is not an accusation, and the work says so on its face: where the ArtBase names a preserved copy, seventy-four of seventy-six keeper addresses answered - what someone took on, held. The gap is between what a catalogue can list and what a keeper has taken on, and for a hundred and twenty-two of these hundred and eighty-eight works the record names no keeper at all, eighty-three of those hundred and twenty-two having no living address of their own either. VERIFIED: every number on the page is derived by build.py from data.json and build.py --check fails on a one-byte drift; the raw responses of both knocks and both archive passes are committed beside the page under evidence/. Four addresses returned a page under a 200 status that an automatic placeholder signal flagged; all four were fetched and read by hand, three were placeholders and one was the work itself, and each adjudication is printed with the sentence it rests on. CORRECTED IN THE RECORD: two errors of this session are stated on the page and in METHOD.md rather than repaired silently - a pilot run that passed an SSL context to a method that does not take one and so reported twenty-four of twenty-four live addresses as unreachable, and a first archive pass that asked once per address and whose eighty failed requests the join read as no snapshot, which would have reported sixty-eight works as found nowhere; asking up to four times, spaced, turned seventy-one of those into snapshots that exist, and the page reports the second pass while stating the first. FLOOR, NOT CLAIM: one knock is not a death certificate, six addresses refused this instrument outright and are counted as not found, and the Internet Archive's CDX index is blocked by this session's egress policy, so the seventeen are no snapshot reported after four asks and not not archived. Answering is also not the same as working: nothing was fetched from inside a work, and two of these addresses serve a file in a format no current browser plays and both answered. NEIGHBOURS AND DAYLIGHT, as the direction of 2026-09-03 requires: in the Atlas, blackaeonium (a keeping-place) by lisa cianci and Digital Decay III by Claire Evans make loss and decay their material, where this page does not perform decay but measures a named corpus at a named hour with its evidence attached; netart_latino database by Brian Mackern builds an index of net art as a work, where this surveys what an existing index still reaches; and Marathon 55 . Cache Memory by Gregory Chatonsky is about a work migrating off the server into the reader's cache, stands in this wall, and is one of the five whose address moved with its maker. Outside the Atlas the neighbour is the reference-rot literature in scholarly communication, which counts decayed links in citations; the daylight is that this counts a second address per work, the keeper's, and reports the two side by side, which a link-rot count cannot do because it has only one address and so cannot tell a work that is gone from a work someone is holding. The page describes what public catalogues and public servers returned to one identified instrument at one hour, quotes the pages it read, and makes no claim about any person's conduct; its subject is what a citation reaches, not who is at fault.
form: interactive, client-rendered, with a complete no-JS floor
